claims.text: The decoupled predictive approach will reduce prediction error by at least 20% relative to traditional Debye or aggregated DFT methods.
A temperature-dependent crossover occurs near 200 K.
Electronic heat transport dominates above approximately 200 K in HfNbTaTiZr.
The lattice contribution becomes increasingly significant as temperature decreases below approximately 200 K.
The approach will provide accurate total thermal-conductivity predictions over approximately 100–1200 K.
The target material is high-purity, homogenized, nominally defect-free HfNbTaTiZr with less than 1 wt.% oxygen.
The proposed model separately computes electronic density of states, electron-phonon coupling, phonon dispersion, and force-constant disorder using ab initio calculations.
Disordered atomic masses and variations in force constants give rise to distinct lattice and electronic thermal-transport contributions.
Independent calculation of electronic parameters and phonon-scattering spectra avoids relying solely on a Debye-temperature approximation.
Capturing atomic-scale disorder and complexity prevents conflation of lattice and electronic thermal transport.
Earlier methods conflate lattice and electronic contributions.
Prior analytical and DFT-based estimates often rely on a single Debye temperature or aggregated elastic properties.
Prior analytical and DFT-based estimates predict high-temperature total conductivity in the range 10–17 W/(K m).
Low-temperature experiments show comparable lattice and electronic contributions.
The prediction applies to defect-free, well-characterized, single-phase HfNbTaTiZr specimens.
Significant impurities, microstructural heterogeneity, or defects will degrade model accuracy.
Model accuracy may deteriorate outside the 100–1200 K range.
Magnetic-field-dependent or combined thermal and electrical measurements can separately quantify lattice and electronic conductivity.
Failure to reduce error by at least 20% relative to baseline methods falsifies the hypothesis.
Failure to predict electronic dominance above approximately 200 K falsifies the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The target is repeatedly called defect-free, but the initial-state definition permits a nonzero oxygen impurity below 1 wt.%; oxygen in solid solution or associated phases is not consistent with a strictly defect-free specimen.
